function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
It sounds like you’re dealing with two different identifier schemes—`culprit_unique_id` from your internal system and `crm_id` from the external CRM—and they don’t match up directly. Here’s a quick checklist on how to bridge that gap: | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **1️⃣ Identify the source** | Confirm which system owns each ID (e.g., your database vs. the CRM). | Knowing the origin helps decide where to store the mapping. | | **2️⃣ Create a mapping table** | Add a new table (or extend an existing one) that stores both IDs side‑by‑side. Example schema:
`id_map`
• `internal_id` (primary key)
• `crm_id`
• `created_at`
• `updated_at` | Keeps a single place to look up either direction. | | **3️⃣ Populate the mapping** | Run a batch job that pulls records from both systems and matches them using other unique fields (email, phone, etc.). | You’ll only have a reliable link if there’s another common attribute. | | **4️⃣ Keep it in sync** | Whenever you create or update a record in either system, also insert/update the corresponding row in `id_map`. | Prevents stale links that could break downstream processes. | | **5️⃣ Use the mapping in queries** | Instead of joining on `culprit_unique_id` ↔ `crm_id`, join on `id_map.internal_id` ↔ `id_map.crm_id`. | Makes the relationship explicit and easier to maintain. | ### Quick example (SQL) ```sql -- Create the mapping table CREATE TABLE id_map ( internal_id VARCHAR(255) PRIMARY KEY, crm_id VARCHAR(255), created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ); -- Insert a new mapping INSERT INTO id_map (internal_id, crm_id) VALUES ('abc123', 'CRM-98765'); -- Update when you get a new CRM ID UPDATE id_map SET crm_id='CRM-54321' WHERE internal_id='abc123'; ``` ### Things to watch out for - **Uniqueness** – Ensure `internal_id` is truly unique in your system; otherwise you’ll get duplicate rows. - **Data quality** – If you rely on email/phone to match, clean those fields first (trim spaces, standardize formats). - **Performance** – Index both columns if you’ll be querying frequently. If you’d like help writing a script to populate this table automatically (e.g., using Python + SQLAlchemy), just let me know!
